opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that when DeepSeek R1 came out, it showed the world that you can get really strong reasoning behavior, but the recipe, especially on the data side, wasn't fully open. You had open weights, but you didn't have the open dataset or a clear understanding of what kind of data actually makes a model reason well. That's the gap we wanted to fill with Open Thoughts.

Open Thoughts is a collaborative effort. We at Bespoke Labs worked with a group of academic researchers, many of whom were involved in DataComp. The goal is to build the best open reasoning datasets and to share everything: the data, the curation pipeline, the code, and the models trained on it. Open Thinker is the family of models we train on that data, partly to show that the data works, and partly to give the community strong, fully open reasoning models they can build on.

I think the contribution happens on a few levels. First, there's the artifact level. People can download the dataset and fine-tune their own models, and we've seen a lot of folks do exactly that. Second, and maybe more importantly, there's the science level. Because everything's open, we can run careful, systematic experiments on questions like: Where should your questions come from? How much does filtering matter? Should you sample multiple answers per question? Does verifying answers help or not? Which teacher model should you distill from? Some of the answers are surprising. For example, a stronger model on benchmarks isn't necessarily a better teacher. Those are the insights that help everyone, not just us.

And third, there's the community side. Reasoning models are moving incredibly fast, and if all the knowledge is locked up in a few big labs, the rest of the field just can't keep up or meaningfully contribute. By making the whole pipeline transparent, we lower the barrier so a university lab or a small startup can actually study reasoning, reproduce results, and push things forward. So I see Open Thoughts as a kind of shared foundation: open data, open recipes, and open models that let the broader community participate in building reasoning models instead of just consuming them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the big picture here is that when DeepSeek-R1 came out, it was a huge moment, because suddenly everyone could see that this kind of reasoning behavior, the long chains of thought, the self-verification, the backtracking, could be distilled into much smaller models. But the actual recipe for how you build that data was still fairly opaque. You got the weights, you got a paper, but you didn't get the data, and you didn't get a lot of the details about what makes a good reasoning dataset versus a mediocre one.

So Open Thoughts is really an attempt to close that gap. It's a collaborative effort, there's folks from Bespoke Labs, Stanford, Berkeley, UW, Toyota Research Institute, and a bunch of others, and the goal is to build the best open reasoning datasets we can and release everything, the data, the models, the code, the evaluations, so people can actually reproduce it and build on it.

And Open Thinker is the family of models we train on top of that data, mostly to validate that the data is good. The first one, OpenThinker-7B, was trained on something like 114K examples that were distilled from R1, and it was already competitive with, or better than, DeepSeek's own distilled 7B on math and code benchmarks. Then we scaled that up to around a million examples with OpenThoughts3, and that got us models at 7B and 32B that are, as far as I know, the strongest open-data reasoning models at those sizes.

But honestly, the part I'm most excited about isn't any individual model, it's the science. We ran something like a thousand ablations on things like: which questions should you even bother asking? Does it matter which teacher model you distill from? Should you filter answers for correctness, or is it fine to just keep everything? And some of the findings were surprising. Verification, for instance, turned out to matter a lot less than people assumed. What mattered much more was the quality and diversity of the questions, and sampling multiple responses per question. QwQ-32B ended up being a better teacher than much bigger models in some settings.

So the contribution, I'd say, is twofold. One is just giving the community strong, fully open reasoning models and the data behind them, so you're not starting from zero. And two, it's turning reasoning data curation into something you can actually study rigorously, rather than a bunch of folklore about what works. Because if the field is going to move from a handful of labs that know the recipe to everyone being able to build these models, that recipe has to be public and it has to be understood.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest contribution is making the development of reasoning models more open and reproducible. With Open Thoughts, the focus is on the data: how do you create examples that teach a model to work through a problem, and how do you make that process available for others to study? Open Thinker is the model side of that effort—using that data to train models that people can run, evaluate, and build on.

Having model weights is useful, but it doesn’t tell you how to reproduce the capabilities. You also want to understand where the data came from, how it was filtered, and which choices actually mattered. Opening up that process lets the community experiment with those questions instead of starting from scratch.

The exciting part is that it creates a feedback loop. Better data leads to better models, and studying where those models fail helps you figure out what data you need next. That gives more researchers a way to contribute to reasoning, even if they don’t have the resources to build a large foundation model themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Open Thoughts and OpenThinker as complementary efforts. Open Thoughts is about making the reasoning data available, and OpenThinker is about showing what you can build with that data. Together, they give the community a way to study and improve reasoning models, rather than just interact with a model through an API.

A big question is what actually makes reasoning training work. How much does data quality matter? How much diversity do you need across math, coding, and other tasks? If the data and the models are open, researchers can run those experiments, compare results, and build on one another’s work. My hope is that this makes progress more accessible and helps us develop a better understanding of where these capabilities come from.
